newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma to blockade opposition while ASEAN meets.
newsitem.headline: Burma to blockade opposition while ASEAN meets.

text.p: Burma's authorities will bar entry to democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi's home and blockade her party's headquarters until after a crucial ASEAN membership meeting this weekend, an official source said on Friday.
He said the military government wanted to avoid clashes with members of the National League for Democracy (NLD), which has urged the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) not to admit Burma.
"They know that the NLD is planning to make some move during the ASEAN meeting, so they are banning people from access to the NLD to deter them from gathering," the source said.
"SLORC (the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council) is applying this deterrent because they want to refrain from using force on the eve of the ASEAN meeting."

NLD sources confirmed that they were planning to hold a meeting or come up with a resolution before the seven-nation group's foreign ministers' meeting in Kuala Lumpur on Saturday to decide when to admit Burma, Cambodia and Laos.
The authorities this week thwarted NLD plans for a mass meeting at Suu Kyi's house to mark the anniversary of the party's 1990 landslide election win, which was not recognised by SLORC.
Security around the 1991 Nobel Peace laureate's University Avenue home was relaxed on Thursday as barbed wire barricades and riot police were withdrawn.
But witnesses said on Friday that police were still stopping traffic from entering the road and two barbed wire barricades were blocking access to the NLD's headquarters in the centre of the capital.
There was no word on the 316 party supporters, including about 50 members of parliament, who the NLD says were arrested in a nationwide swoop to stop the congress taking place.
The government denies charges it has detained party members and has asked the NLD to prove its claims.

ASEAN -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- has already decided to admit its three last members as a group this year. The foreign ministers' meeting is to decide exactly when.

Malaysia, this year's ASEAN chairman, has pressed for the three to be inducted at the association's annual ministerial meeting, which is scheduled for July 24-25. Another proposal would be to admit them at an informal ASEAN summit in December.
The United States has asked ASEAN to delay Burma's entry because of its human rights record and the suppression of Suu Kyi's movement.

ASEAN nations have objected to what they see as Washington's interference in its affairs. However, Western diplomats say recent signs of instability in Burma, including moves to stop the NLD congress, had caused some to rethink. Suu Kyi, in a taped interview that was smuggled out of the country and released on Thursday, warned that Burma's military rulers could become "even more obdurate and oppressive" if the country were admitted to ASEAN.
She said that Burma, under the rule of SLORC, would be no credit to ASEAN and called on the group to engage with her party.
